extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, critics, translators, and educated readers of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for composing, translating, and judging poetry and drama (esp. tragedy, epic, and comedy), covering imitation, plot, character, language, music, spectacle, and related principles. Includes criteria for arrangement, plausibility, and the effects a work should produce (pity, terror, catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation (mimesis) and its means
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry and the imitatives arts are defined by imitation; they differ by the means they use to imitate (rhythm, language, harmony, or mixes thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: flute/lyre use rhythm and harmony; dance imitates by rhythm alone and can imitate manners, passions, actions; epic/epopee uses language or verse (often one measure); some genres (dithyrambics, nomoi, tragedy, comedy) employ rhythm, melody, and verse together, though in different parts. The means of imitation helps determine the species of the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects of imitation (who/what is imitated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts differ by the things imitated: persons may be represented as better than they are, worse, or as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer forms characters better; Cleophon as they are; some writers (e.g., Nicocharis) make them worse. These choices affect whether a work tends toward tragedy, comedy, epic, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of imitation (how it is imitated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation can be by simple narration, by assuming characters, or by representation through actors; the same objects and means can be imitated in different manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Homer alternates between narration and assumed character; drama uses persons acting. The manner (narration vs enacted) is a key formal distinction among genres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is an imitation of an important and complete action, of a certain magnitude, in ornamented language, having distinct parts, by representation of persons acting (not by narration), effecting through pity and fear the purgation (catharsis) of such passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key components to check: importance and completeness of action, magnitude, ornamented language (rhythm, harmony, measure), enactment rather than narration, and the work's effect on pity and terror (catharsis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Six constituent parts of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy has six parts: fable (plot), character (manners), thought/sentiment, diction (language), melody (music), and spectacle (scenery/decorations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order of importance: plot (fable) is primary, then character, then thought, diction, melody, spectacle. Each part has a role: plot is the imitation of action; character determines actions; thought reveals intentions/opinions; diction is the expression; melody and spectacle assist the representation (spectacle least dependent on poet).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of plot (fable) over character
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot (combination of incidents) is the imitation of action and is the chief cause of tragic pleasure; character is secondary and exists to support the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether incidents are arranged to produce a coherent causal sequence with beginning, middle, and end; characters should be judged on how well they serve the plot rather than vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single, complete action)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must represent a single, complete action — an integral whole with a beginning, middle, and end — not a mere succession of episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thefable should be compact (if expanded like an epic it becomes languid), and not compound different actions that break unity. Unity of action is 'rigidly observed' and judged against the standard of natural cause-and-effect linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex versus simple plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are complex when they include reversal (peripeteia) and/or recognition (anagnorisis); simple when lacking these events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that produce these transformations (reversal/recognition) are superior because they generate stronger emotional effects (pity/fear) and a more striking catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peripeteia is a change by which actions veer around to the opposite, producing a reversal of fortune in the plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best when reversal is probable or necessary and arises from the plot's causal structure rather than caprice. Reversal often pairs with recognition to intensify catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (recognition/discovery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Anagnorisis is the change from ignorance to knowledge, where a character recognizes a previously unknown fact, identity, or relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combined with peripeteia, recognition heightens emotional impact; the most effective recognitions are those that logically arise from the plot's causal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathos (suffering) and its role
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathos — destructive or painful events (suffering) — is one of the elements that a tragedy may employ to move pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffering should arise from the plot's necessities and be proportionate to maintain plausibility and avoid gratuitous horror; it functions within the mechanism that produces catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability, Necessity, and Plausibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in the plot should follow from necessity or probability (or likeness to reality); impossible or gratuitously absurd events are faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticisms against impossibility or absurdity can sometimes be excused if the plot is made more interesting, or if the poet describes things as they ought to be rather than as they are, or from ignorance; but in general probability and causal necessity are required for a good plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catharsis (purgation of pity and fear)
rubrics_metrics.description: A central end of tragedy is to arouse pity and terror and to effect a purgation, cleansing, or unburdening of these passions in the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the incidents, reversals, and recognitions provoked the appropriate affective response and whether the overall emotional discharge is achieved without relying on spectacle alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character requirements (qualities of persons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be consistent, appropriate, and true to type: they should be good (to some degree), fitting to their station, and exhibit uniformity of character across actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A tragic protagonist should not be wholly vicious nor perfectly virtuous; flaws (errors) should be humanizing and causally linked to the plot. Evaluate propriety of speech and acts for each character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamartia (tragic error or flaw)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic misfortune often arises from an error of judgment (hamartia) or a mistake rather than from vice or depravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The error should be plausible, avoid making the character wholly blameworthy, and serve to produce pity and fear; intentional wickedness is less fitting for eliciting catharsis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate diction and excellence of language
rubrics_metrics.description: Language should be ornamented (accompanied by rhythm, harmony, and measure); excellence of diction includes proper nouns, metaphors, accent, and division of sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style must suit the characters and situation (propriety). Metaphor and novel expression are praised when apt; foreign words, bad accent, or misplaced punctuation can be grounds for criticism unless excused by necessary poetic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of metaphor and figures of speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is important for excellence of style and for conveying thought vividly; choice of metaphors affects clarity and novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess metaphors for aptness, intelligibility, and their contribution to the emotional and intellectual impact of the lines; unnecessary obscurity or forced ornamentation is a fault.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhythm, harmony, and measure in language
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of tragedy employ verse with rhythm and measure; some parts require the aid of music while others rely on verse alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iambic measure is especially suited to dramatic discourse (closer to speech), while hexameter suits epic. The poet should choose meters consistent with the genre and function of the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of melody (music) and chorus
rubrics_metrics.description: Melody (music) and the chorus contribute to the imitation and are constituent parts of tragedy, assisting but being less dependent on the poet's skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Music and choral composition should harmonize with the dramatic purpose; though important to spectators, they are not the poet's primary craft, which is construction of the fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle and stage decoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenery, costume, and visual effects (spectacle) are constituent parts of drama, and though least dependent on the poet, they are often most striking to the spectator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacle can heighten effect but should not substitute for plot and character; flaws in spectacle do not absolve failures in the core poetic elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of time and place (temporal/spatial limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a boundary fixed to the duration of the dramatic action (unity of time) — stricter in ancient drama because the stage is continuously occupied by actors and chorus; unity of place was common but not universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On ancient practice, extension of time beyond the performance's apparent duration strains probability; modern stages may allow greater assumed time lapses without offending taste, but unity of action remains decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement of incidents (plot ordering)
rubrics_metrics.description: The order and method of arranging incidents (what ought to be attempted in the arrangement of the fable) determine how effectively the proper end of tragedy is attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange incidents so causes lead naturally to effects; produce a plausible and necessary sequence that yields a coherent beginning, middle, and end and facilitates peripeteia/recognition where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: How pity and terror are excited
rubrics_metrics.description: Pity and terror are excited by the plot's incidents, the protagonist's misfortune (especially when arising from error), and the combination of reversal and recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To generate pity and terror, contrive events that are probable and necessary, show the protagonist's humanity, and time revelations to maximize emotional impact without violating plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Errors and objections of criticism (five species)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticisms of a poem reduce to five species: the impossible, the absurd, the hurtful, the contradictory, and errors against the rules of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some faults may be excused (if they make the poem more interesting, stem from ignorance, depict things as they ought to be, reflect received opinion, or arise from character circumstances). Consider context, character, and poet's intent before censuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference between epic and tragic imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic imitation is narrative, longer in duration, and more adapted to the vulgar (requiring spectacle/action to be intelligible); tragedy is condensed, enacted, more unified, and often superior in effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing forms, check unity, condensation of time, and whether the work achieves its end (including catharsis) more effectively in its chosen mode of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic criteria (nature of comedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy imitates worse people — not wicked in general but those subject to ridicule via mistakes of judgment or deformities (not caused by pain); its aim is ridicule rather than purgation of pity/terror.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy's objects differ from tragedy's; evaluate comedic works by their success in producing laughter through appropriate targets (mistake, deformity) and by avoiding malicious personal invective when a fable/general subject is intended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of measure and its suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain measures suit certain genres: iambic is most calculated for dialogue and dramatic discourse; hexameter belongs to epic; mixing many measures for heroic subjects is absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a measure appropriate to the function (iambic for speech-like dialogue, hexameter for narrative epic) and avoid incongruous mixtures that disrupt the nature of the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character propriety and uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should show uniformity and propriety — their language and actions must be consistent with their social role, status, and temperament.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether utterances are what a 'sensible man may deliver' in those circumstances; if not, consider whether the character's nature or the exigencies of the plot justify the speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and defense of departures from strict realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Departures from actuality may be permitted when they make the poem more interesting, serve a moral or artistic 'ought', reflect common belief, or are necessitated by the character or circumstances of speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging questionable incidents or expressions, consider whether they are artistic choices that improve the whole and whether the audience can accept them given the work's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translational principle: perspicuity over literalness
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating, aim to render clearly what is conceived to be the original meaning, as nearly in the original words as is consistent with perspicuity; paraphrase literal passages that would be obscure to a modern reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator's practice: avoid attempting elegance of style; prefer clarity; use notes to explain difficult passages or justify readings; in corrupted texts, use reasonable paraphrase and conjecture to restore sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling corrupted texts and fragmentary quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ancient texts are corrupted or present fragments of poets; rendering such passages intelligible may require considerable liberty in paraphrase and conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translator/commentator should study available editions and commentators, acknowledge conjectures, and use examples/paraphrase to make otherwise unintelligible fragments accessible to readers.
